name: Claret
lede: Claret is a deep reddish purple named after red Bordeaux wine.

sections.title: A wine's name
sections.body:
Paterson describes claret as reddish-violet, the color of claret wine, and as a red with the same hue as [[bordeaux]] wine [1]. It gives the wine word a Latin source, *clarus*, "clear", the root of clarity, clarinet and clarion [1]. That is the dictionary's etymology, offered without further evidence [1].

The dictionary's two descriptions, reddish-violet and a red of bordeaux hue, differ a little [1]. In our measure the nearest wine name is [[burgundy]], 5.9 units away [3].

sections.title: In cloth and fashion
sections.body:
The word has long served in textile description. A V&A monograph on Kashmir shawl fragments describes one pattern, with white roses, in a list of colors that runs straw, saxe blue, green muscat, claret and mole [2]. A newspaper account of the Milan collections in February 2000 lists a claret velvet tailored jacket in a season that also brought mauve back, alongside a purple trouser suit and a streamlined camel car coat [4]. In that company claret reads as a deep, fashionable wine tone worn in fabric, not a pigment from a painter's box.

Our library gives claret an entry in the ISCC-NBS lists of 1955 and the Maerz and Paul dictionary [3]. It also sits near [[wine-red]], [[maroon]] and [[oxblood]], which name similar dark reds [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Claret is rare in our archive of 23,781 paintings: it appears in 11, about 0.05%, as photographed, and it is rarer than 65% of the named colors [3]. Inside a painting it is mostly an accent, in 86% of the 14 paintings measured by lightness rank [3]. The earliest match is a work of 1518 by Bartolomeo di Zanobi di Benedetto Ghetti, a floor in a thin early archive [3].

That is 437 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, 1955, so the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of a wine-dark pigment [3].
